runs.text:
A generation begins with three files: a style guide, a corpus passage, and a prompt template. The runner parses the frontmatter of each file, hashes the entire file, and records the hash alongside the output.

The guide's body becomes the system prompt. The runner substitutes the passage into the template to form the user prompt. It writes this prompt to the child process on standard input rather than passing it as an argument. As a result, no shell quoting rule and no command-line length limit applies to it.

The runner then spawns the Claude Code command-line interface (CLI) with an explicit argument vector and requests a JSON envelope in response. It waits for the process to complete, using a timeout that escalates from a polite termination signal to a forced kill.

The runner parses the response even when the process exits with a non-zero status code, because a refusal arrives in this form: a failing exit code paired with a well-formed envelope that names the reason. The runner writes every field of that envelope to disk, whether the generation succeeds or fails. It also records the argument vector, the resolved model, the token counts, and the wall-clock duration.

argv:
Rewrite the text following Google's developer documentation style.

Write in the second person and the present tense. Use the active voice and
standard American spelling. Keep the tone precise and even-handed rather than
casual — this is documentation, not conversation. Write complete sentences;
do not use fragments for effect, and do not use contractions.

Prefer short sentences and short paragraphs. Use a numbered list for a
sequence of steps and a bulleted list for an unordered set. Begin each list
item with a capital letter.

Avoid the words "simply", "easily", "just", "obviously", and "of course": what
is obvious to the writer is rarely obvious to the reader. Do not use
placeholder words like "please" in instructions. Avoid metaphors, idioms, and
cultural references that will not translate, and avoid asides or personality
that could distract a reader who is scanning for an answer.

Use inclusive, unambiguous language and spell out an abbreviation on first
use. When in doubt, prefer the more explicit and fully spelled-out phrasing
over the more familiar-sounding one.
